title: How Does MoRo Navigate?
contentStatus: REVISED per Content Principles (60% pass, terminology + notes). Navigation accuracy corrected to variant-specific figures per CDD (±10mm A-250/A-500, ±20mm A-1200). Sensor range, cable-detection threshold, and object-size threshold removed — unverified, no confirmed source.

sections.title: From What to How
learningObjectives: Recall MoRo's core identity from Module 1
Understand why navigation is the technology worth examining next
sections.content: Module 1 established what MoRo is: an autonomous mobile robot that navigates without fixed paths or floor markers. That claim raises an obvious question — how does it actually know where it is? This module answers that directly, covering the sensor technology and the localization process that together let MoRo move through a factory it was never explicitly programmed with a map of in advance.

keyTerms.note: An older category of automated vehicle that follows a fixed path, typically magnetic tape or a buried wire, requiring floor modification.

sections.title: LiDAR — How MoRo Senses Its Surroundings
learningObjectives: Define LiDAR and explain its basic operating principle
Understand what LiDAR can and cannot reliably detect
sections.content: LiDAR (Light Detection and Ranging) is a sensor that emits laser light and measures the time it takes to return after reflecting off a surface, calculating distance from that measurement. MoRo uses this continuously to detect walls, machines, pillars, and people around it. LiDAR has known physical limitations: it detects solid, reflective surfaces reliably, but struggles with transparent materials (glass) and highly reflective or mirror-like surfaces, since these don't reflect the laser predictably back to the sensor. Very fine or low-profile objects at floor level are also harder to detect reliably than larger obstacles. Precise range and detection specifications for MoRo's LiDAR configuration are being confirmed against current hardware documentation and will be added once verified.

keyTerms.note: Light Detection and Ranging — a sensor that measures distance using reflected laser light.

sections.title: SLAM — Locating Itself While Mapping
learningObjectives: Define SLAM and its two component processes
Understand why SLAM enables navigation without fixed infrastructure
sections.content: SLAM (Simultaneous Localization and Mapping) is the process combining two tasks MoRo performs at once: localization (determining its own position) and mapping (building a representation of its surroundings). Neither happens in isolation — MoRo uses what it's mapped to figure out where it is, and uses its estimated position to keep refining the map. This is what eliminates the need for floor tape, magnetic strips, or any other physical infrastructure that older AGV systems required.

keyTerms.note: The combined process of determining one's own position while building a map of the environment, performed continuously and together.
Determining one's own position within a known or partially known environment.

sections.title: Navigation Accuracy
learningObjectives: Know MoRo's confirmed navigation accuracy by variant
Understand that accuracy differs across the product line
sections.content: Navigation accuracy is not identical across all three MoRo variants. The A-250 and A-500 are rated at ±10mm positioning accuracy; the A-1200 is rated at ±20mm — the larger variant's accuracy is intentionally wider, reflecting its different operating profile. This distinction matters operationally: don't assume the same precision applies uniformly across every unit on the floor without checking which variant you're working with.

keyTerms.note: How precisely MoRo can determine and maintain its actual physical position, expressed as a margin of error.

sections.title: Map Creation and Updates
learningObjectives: Understand the general process of building an initial map
Know that maps require periodic updates as the factory changes
sections.content: Before MoRo operates independently in a space, an initial mapping pass is required — the unit is guided through the area to build its baseline map using LiDAR and SLAM. Once established, this map isn't permanent: if the factory layout changes (equipment relocated, new obstacles introduced), the map needs updating to reflect reality. The specific update cadence and process will be confirmed against DiFacto's operational guidance and added here once verified.

sections.title: What This Means for You
learningObjectives: Understand the practical implication of sensor-based navigation for floor personnel
Recognize what to be mindful of given LiDAR's known limitations
sections.content: Because MoRo's navigation depends on LiDAR detecting solid, reflective surfaces, be mindful of what it may not reliably register — transparent barriers, highly reflective surfaces, and very low-profile floor obstructions. This isn't a flaw to be anxious about; it's simply how the sensing technology works, and it's the same reasoning behind the interactive zone and safety behaviors covered in Module 4. Understanding the technology builds appropriate trust — not blind trust, not undue suspicion.

questions.question: What does LiDAR measure to determine distance?
options: The time for emitted laser light to reflect back
questions.feedback: Correct. LiDAR calculates distance from the return time of reflected laser light.

questions.question: What does SLAM stand for?
questions.feedback: Correct. SLAM combines localization and mapping, performed simultaneously.

questions.question: Which type of surface is LiDAR least reliable at detecting?
questions.feedback: Correct. Transparent and highly reflective surfaces don't reflect laser light predictably.

questions.question: What is MoRo's navigation accuracy for the A-1200 variant?
questions.feedback: Correct. The A-1200 is rated at ±20mm, wider than the ±10mm rating for A-250/A-500.

questions.question: Does MoRo's map of a space stay fixed permanently once created?
options: Only if the robot is restarted
No — it requires updates as the factory layout changes
questions.feedback: Correct. Maps need periodic updates to stay accurate as the environment changes.
